segments.text: Structural geology studies how rocks deform under stress, and plate tectonics explains the large-scale forces that drive this deformation across the Earth’s surface — together, they explain the “why” behind the mountain ranges, earthquake zones, and volcanic belts introduced descriptively in Chapter 1.
Stress
is force applied per unit area on a rock (compressive, tensile, or shear, depending on direction relative to the rock surface);
strain
is the resulting deformation. Rock responds to stress in stages depending on the stress magnitude and the conditions (temperature, pressure, rate of loading):
elastic
deformation is temporary and fully reversible if stress is removed (Physics Chapter II’s elasticity concept applied to rock);
plastic
deformation is permanent but does not involve fracturing (typical of rock deep in the crust, under high temperature and confining pressure, deforming slowly, similar to folding); and
brittle
deformation is permanent deformation via fracturing (typical of rock nearer the surface, under lower temperature and pressure, deforming rapidly).
Folds
are bends in rock layers produced by plastic (ductile) deformation, typically under compressive stress. An
anticline
is an upward, arch-like fold (with the oldest rock layers at its core, once eroded), while a
syncline

is a downward, trough-like fold (with the youngest rock layers at its core). Folds are further classified by their symmetry (symmetrical versus asymmetrical, depending on whether both limbs dip at equal angles) and by the orientation of their fold axis (plunging if the axis is tilted, non-plunging if horizontal) — correctly recognising a fold’s geometry from a geological map is essential for interpreting the underlying rock structure and history of deformation.
Faults
are fractures along which rock on either side has moved relative to the other, produced by brittle deformation. The three basic types are classified by the relative direction of movement: a
normal fault
(the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall, typically caused by tensional/extensional stress, common at divergent boundaries), a
reverse fault
(the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall, typically caused by compressional stress, common at convergent boundaries — a
thrust fault
is a specific low-angle reverse fault), and a
strike-slip fault
(movement is predominantly horizontal, parallel to the fault’s strike, associated with transform boundaries, point 6).
Joints

are fractures in rock along which little or no relative movement has occurred (distinguishing them from faults). They commonly form from stress release (such as when overlying rock is eroded away, releasing confining pressure) or from cooling and contraction (particularly notable in some igneous rocks, producing distinctive, regularly spaced columnar joint patterns). Joints significantly influence rock permeability (relevant to groundwater and petroleum geology, later chapters) and weathering patterns, since they provide pathways for water and weathering agents to penetrate the rock mass.

blocks.text: 5. Strike and dip; geological map interpretation

segments.text: Strike
is the compass direction of the line formed by the intersection of an inclined rock layer with a horizontal plane;
dip

is the angle of steepest inclination of that layer, measured downward from horizontal, in the direction perpendicular to the strike. Together, strike and dip fully and precisely describe the three-dimensional orientation of a planar rock layer, and are the essential basic data recorded in the field and shown on geological maps (using standardised symbols) — from which the underlying subsurface rock structure (folds, faults, and their geometry) can be reliably inferred and drawn as a cross-section.

blocks.text: 6. Plate tectonics, plate boundaries, and large-scale tectonic features

segments.text: Plate tectonics

explains the Earth’s large-scale surface deformation as the result of rigid lithospheric plates moving relative to each other, driven ultimately by mantle convection. Three types of plate boundaries produce systematically different geological features:
divergent boundaries
(plates move apart, characteristically producing mid-ocean ridges and normal faulting, along with basaltic volcanism),
convergent boundaries

(plates move together, characteristically producing subduction zones with associated deep earthquakes and explosive volcanism, or mountain-building collision zones where continental plates meet, along with reverse/thrust faulting), and
transform boundaries

(plates slide horizontally past each other, characteristically producing strike-slip faulting and shallow earthquakes, with comparatively little volcanism). This framework directly explains why earthquakes, volcanoes, and specific fault/fold types (points 2 and 3) are geographically concentrated in specific, predictable global belts rather than distributed randomly.

items.text: Rock deforms elastically (reversible), plastically (permanent, no fracture), or brittlely (permanent, with fracture), depending on stress conditions, temperature, pressure, and rate.
Anticlines (upward, older core) and synclines (downward, younger core) are the basic fold types, produced by plastic deformation under compression.
Normal, reverse, and strike-slip faults are distinguished by relative movement direction and are each characteristically associated with a specific type of stress and plate boundary.
Strike and dip together fully describe a rock layer’s three-dimensional orientation and are the essential data underlying geological map interpretation.

The three plate boundary types (divergent, convergent, transform) each produce a characteristic, predictable combination of faulting, folding, seismicity, and volcanism, explaining the global distribution of these features.
